tone.quote: Foe (East Kutubu), sandwiched between Kewa and Fasu, appears to have word tone with just two melodies, high (HL when utterance-final) and low (LHL when utterance-final) (Rule 1993: 24-25). There is no mention of accent in the admittedly scanty account, and this language may form a typological bridge between the word tone of Kewa and the pitch accent of Fasu.

tone.quote: (d) TONE. Tone is also present in the language, with a change of key or tone on the same word making a change in the meaning. Fortunately there are only two tone patterns, and these are superimposed over the whole word. These two patterns are: 1. a lower tone on each of the syllables, with the final syllable going to a high tone & then falling down to low if it is the final word in the sentence. 2. a high tone on each syllable of the word, dropping down on the final syllable if that word is the last in a clause [...] It is therefore clear that tone & stress have to be taken together as a unit.
tone.locator: 'Language' chapter, sections (d) TONE and (e) STRESS & INTONATION, pp. 23-25 as cited by Donohue 2005 and Weiner & Niles 2015 (IA index)
tone.n_tones: 2 word-tone patterns (low melody with final rise vs. all-high), i.e. a two-way…
tone.says: Foe has tone: 'only two tone patterns.. superimposed over the whole word' -- (1) low on each syllable with the final syllable rising to high (falling to low sentence-finally), (2) high on each syllable, dropping on the final syllable clause-finally; minimal pairs (bare 'canoe' vs bare 'tree fern', duru..); high-tone words marked with an acute in the dictionary; stress said to coincide with high tone ('tone & stress have to be taken together as a unit'). Basis: scanned search snippets of pp. 23-…
